lesson.title: The Y-Coordinate: Rising and Falling on the Plane
lesson.summary: The y-coordinate is the second number in an ordered pair, and it tells you how far to move up or down from the origin.
lesson.body:
If the x-coordinate answers "how far left or right," the y-coordinate answers the other half of the question: "how far up or down?" Every ordered pair (x, y) needs both answers to describe a single point, because a flat plane has two independent directions of movement, and one number can only describe one of them. The y-coordinate is always the second number in the pair, and its entire purpose is to measure vertical position relative to the horizontal axis, the same way the x-coordinate measures horizontal position relative to the vertical axis.

Just like the x-coordinate, the sign of the y-coordinate is meaningful rather than arbitrary. A positive y-coordinate places the point above the horizontal axis, and a negative y-coordinate places it below. A y-coordinate of zero means the point has no vertical displacement at all, so it must sit exactly on the horizontal axis. This is the same logic used for the x-coordinate, just rotated ninety degrees: one axis handles side to side, the other handles up and down, and the y-coordinate is the up-and-down report. If you isolate the y-axis by itself, it behaves like its own number line, with the y-coordinate telling you where a point falls along it.

Because position in the pair matters, it helps to practice reading pairs consistently: in (x, y), the first number is always horizontal movement, and the second is always vertical movement. Mixing this up is one of the most common early errors, since (4, -3) and (-3, 4) look similar but describe points in completely different places, in fact in different quadrants entirely. Keeping the phrase "x first, y second" in mind avoids that mistake entirely, and it is worth repeating until it becomes automatic.

Here is a worked example. Two points share the same x-coordinate, so they sit on the same vertical line: point C is (4, 2) and point D is (4, y). If D is known to be 5 units above C, then y = 2 + 5 = 7, because moving up adds to the y-coordinate. Check this by measuring the vertical distance between the two y-coordinates: |7 - 2| = 5, which matches the given distance. So D is the point (4, 7). As a second check, since D is above C, its y-coordinate should be the larger of the two, and 7 is indeed greater than 2, so the direction of the result makes sense too. Notice how this mirrors the x-coordinate example from the previous chapter almost exactly, just rotated from horizontal movement to vertical movement.

Together, the x-coordinate and y-coordinate form a complete ordered pair, and neither one alone can locate a point. This partnership is what makes the coordinate plane so powerful: once you know how far to go horizontally and how far to go vertically, you can find any point at all, which is exactly the skill needed for plotting points and reading graphs in the chapters ahead.
